questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a hypopigmented anaesthetic patch on his forearm with thickened ulnar nerve. Slit skin smear shows 3+ bacillary index. Which type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: High bacillary index (3+) with nerve thickening and hypopigmented patches is characteristic of borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy. Pure lepromatous leprosy (LL) has even higher BI (5-6+) and diffuse skin infiltration without well-defined patches.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden painful erythematous nodules all over the body with fever, malaise, and iridocyclitis. ESR is elevated. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.exp: This is Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL / Type 2 reaction) occurring in BL/LL leprosy. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for ENL. MDT must NOT be stopped. Steroids are used for ENL with neuritis or iridocyclitis but thalidomide is first-line for uncomplicated severe ENL.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with a history of SLE presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin, sparing mucous membranes. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin in elderly, but can occur in young patients with SLE. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ (hemidesmosomes, anti-BP180 and BP230). EBA also shows linear IgG but targets type VII collagen and is associated with IBD.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with painful erosions of the oral mucosa for 3 months followed by flaccid bullae on the trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells. DIF shows intercellular IgG ('fish net' pattern). What is the pathological mechanism?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris involves IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (skin). Loss of cell-cell adhesion causes suprabasal acantholysis, flaccid bullae, positive Nikolsky sign, and positive Tzanck smear. DIF shows intercellular IgG in a 'chicken wire/fish net' pattern.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. She also has a history of celiac disease. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blister with neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillae. Best treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is associated with celiac disease/gluten sensitivity. DIF shows pathognomonic granular IgA at dermal papillae tips. Treatment is dapsone for rapid itch relief plus lifelong gluten-free diet. G6PD must be checked before dapsone.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening of face and hands, telangiectasias, and heartburn. HRCT shows honeycomb fibrosis. ANA is positive with anti-Scl-70 antibody. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and predicts pulmonary fibrosis. CREST syndrome (limited SSc) is associated with anti-centromere antibodies. The presence of pulmonary fibrosis and anti-Scl-70 favors dcSSc.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with photosensitive facial rash (sparing nasolabial folds), discoid lesions, oral ulcers, and joint pain. ANA 1:640, anti-dsDNA positive, C3/C4 low. Which skin finding is pathognomonic for SLE?
opts: None of the above — no single finding is pathognomonic
questions.exp: No single skin finding is pathognomonic for SLE. The malar (butterfly) rash spares nasolabial folds and is characteristic but not pathognomonic. Discoid lesions can occur in isolated discoid lupus. Gottron's papules are pathognomonic for dermatomyositis, not SLE. Diagnosis requires ACR/EULAR criteria.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, and V-sign on the chest. CK is markedly elevated. What investigation is most important to perform next?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults over 40 is strongly associated with underlying malignancy (15-30%), especially ovarian, lung, colorectal, and nasopharyngeal carcinomas. A thorough malignancy workup (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, tumor markers, colonoscopy) is mandatory at diagnosis. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome.

questions.q: A 28-year-old with severe plaque psoriasis fails methotrexate. He is started on a biologic. After 2 weeks he develops numerous small pustular lesions all over the trunk and extremities, with fever and leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: AGEP (Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis) can be triggered by drugs including biologic agents. It presents with sudden eruption of non-follicular sterile pustules on erythematous skin, fever, and leukocytosis within days to weeks of drug exposure. It resolves with desquamation on stopping the drug.

questions.q: A 20-year-old on carbamazepine for epilepsy develops widespread erythema, target lesions, erosions of two or more mucous membranes, and epidermal detachment involving >30% BSA. What is this condition and its mortality predictor?
questions.exp: Epidermal detachment >30% BSA with two or more mucosal sites = Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). SJS has <10% BSA detachment. SCORTEN (SCORe of TEN) is validated for predicting mortality in TEN, incorporating age, heart rate, malignancy, BUN, glucose, bicarbonate, and affected BSA.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly nodule with telangiectasias on the nose that has been slowly growing for 2 years. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel structures. Histology shows peripheral palisading of nuclei with retraction artefact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy. Nodular BCC on the nose: pearly surface, telangiectasias, spoke-wheel structures on dermoscopy, and peripheral nuclear palisading with retraction artefact histologically are classic. It almost never metastasizes but is locally invasive.

questions.q: A 65-year-old with longstanding burn scar on the lower limb develops a rapidly growing, tender ulcerated nodule with indurated borders. Biopsy shows atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls. This carcinoma arising in a scar is called?
questions.exp: Marjolin's ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic scar, ulcer, or burn wound. It is more aggressive than de novo SCC with higher rates of metastasis. Bowen's disease is SCC in situ. Bazex syndrome (acrokeratosis paraneoplastica) presents with psoriasiform lesions on acral sites with internal malignancy.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4=80) presents with painless, violaceous papules and plaques on the lower limbs, oral mucosa, and trunk. Histology shows spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated RBCs, and plasma cells. What is the aetiological agent?
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (Human Herpesvirus 8, also called KSHV). It is an angioproliferative tumour seen in severely immunocompromised patients. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, PAS-positive hyaline globules, and plasma cells.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 10-year history of a pruritic, erythematous, scaly plaque on the thigh that does not respond to topical steroids. Skin biopsy shows epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier's microabscesses. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. It progresses through patch, plaque, and tumour stages. Pautrier's microabscesses (intraepidermal clusters of atypical cerebriform lymphocytes) are pathognomonic. Sézary syndrome is leukaemic MF with Sézary cells in peripheral blood.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active woman presents with painless genital ulcers and bilateral painless inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). The ulcer base is clean, non-purulent. RPR positive 1:64, TPHA positive. What is the stage of syphilis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents with the classic painless chancre (clean base, indurated edges) and bilateral non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. RPR and TPHA confirm T. pallidum infection. Secondary syphilis occurs 4-10 weeks after primary and presents with maculopapular rash on palms/soles, condylomata lata, and mucous patches.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with painful genital ulcers with undermined, ragged edges and soft base, and unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain of ulcer exudate shows 'school of fish' arrangement of gram-negative coccobacilli. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful soft ulcers with ragged edges and tender unilateral bubo. Gram stain shows 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. Azithromycin 1g single dose or Ceftriaxone 250mg IM are first-line treatments per current STI guidelines.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with large, painless, beefy-red, non-tender ulcerative lesions on the vulva and perineum. No lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows Donovan bodies within mononuclear cells on Giemsa stain. What is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Donovanosis (Granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Classic presentation: painless, beefy-red, friable ulcers without lymphadenopathy; Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic organisms in macrophages) on Giemsa stain. Azithromycin 1g weekly for 3+ weeks (or 500mg daily) is currently recommended first-line treatment.

questions.q: A 25-year-old with LGV (Lymphogranuloma venereum) presents with tender inguinal buboes. The 'groove sign of Greenblatt' is noted. What is the causative agent and its serotype?
questions.exp: LGV is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3. The groove sign of Greenblatt (inguinal lymphadenopathy above and below Poupart's ligament divided by it) is pathognomonic. Serovars D-K cause non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU). Treatment is doxycycline 100mg BD for 21 days.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusts around the mouth and nose. No fever, superficial erosions underneath the crusts. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the most common causative organism?
questions.exp: Impetigo contagiosa presents with honey-colored crusts on the face. Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase-positive, phage group II) is the most common causative organism, though mixed infections with Streptococcus pyogenes occur. Treatment: topical mupirocin or oral anti-staphylococcal antibiotics for widespread cases.

questions.q: A neonate develops widespread superficial blistering, skin peeling like wet tissue paper, and positive Nikolsky sign. No mucosal involvement. What toxin is responsible for this condition?
opts: Exfoliative toxin A and B from Staphylococcus aureus
questions.exp: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS/Ritter disease in neonates) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (serines proteases) from S. aureus phage group II. Toxins cleave desmoglein 1 causing superficial (subcorneal) cleavage. No mucosal involvement (unlike TEN). Treatment: IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

questions.q: A 35-year-old immunocompromised man on systemic steroids presents with a pruritic scaly annular lesion on the groin with active scaling at the border and central clearing. KOH mount shows branching septate hyphae. What is the first-line oral antifungal?
questions.exp: Tinea cruris (caused by Trichophyton rubrum, T. mentagrophytes) is a dermatophyte infection of the groin. Terbinafine (allylamine) is fungicidal and first-line oral treatment for dermatophytosis. Fluconazole is azole (fungistatic). Nystatin is ineffective against dermatophytes. Amphotericin is for systemic fungal infections.

questions.q: A young adult presents with hypopigmented macules on the chest and back that fluoresce golden-yellow under Wood's lamp. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and M. globosa). KOH mount shows clusters of round spores and short curved hyphae — the classic 'spaghetti (hyphae) and meatballs (spores)' pattern. Wood's lamp: golden-yellow fluorescence. Treatment: topical selenium sulfide, ketoconazole, or single-dose oral itraconazole 400mg.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with a large verrucous plaque on the face with satellite lesions. India ink preparation of CSF shows encapsulated yeast. Skin biopsy shows mucicarmine-positive organisms with minimal inflammatory reaction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated yeast) causes cryptococcosis in immunocompromised patients. Skin manifestations: molluscum-like papules, ulcers, or cellulitis. India ink prep shows capsule. Mucicarmine stains the capsule red (pathognomonic). Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is most common presentation in AIDS.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome on the right side, associated with severe burning pain. What is the drug of choice and optimal timing for initiation?
opts: Acyclovir within 72 hours of rash onset
Valacyclovir within 72 hours of rash onset
Famciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset
Either valacyclovir or famciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (caused by VZV reactivation) should be treated within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce severity and risk of postherpetic neuralgia. Valacyclovir 1g TDS for 7 days and famciclovir 500mg TDS for 7 days are preferred over acyclovir for better bioavailability and dosing convenience. Both are equivalent.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with multiple flesh-colored, dome-shaped umbilicated papules on the trunk and limbs. Giemsa-stained smear of expressed content shows large cytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies). What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (caused by poxvirus MCV-1 in children, MCV-2 in adults/STD) presents with umbilicated papules. Henderson-Paterson bodies are pathognomonic inclusion bodies on histology. Treatment: physical destruction methods (curettage, cryotherapy, podophyllotoxin). Spontaneous resolution can occur in immunocompetent children.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops scaly red plaques with well-defined borders on the scalp, elbows, and knees. Biopsy shows acanthosis, elongation of rete ridges (test-tube in rack), suprapapillary thinning, and Munro's microabscesses. The Auspitz sign is positive. Which cytokine axis is primarily targeted by biologic therapies?
questions.exp: Psoriasis is a Th17-mediated disease driven by the IL-23/Th17 axis. IL-23 promotes Th17 differentiation; IL-17A drives keratinocyte proliferation and neutrophil recruitment. Biologics targeting this axis include IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-17RA inhibitor (brodalumab), and IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab). TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept) are older agents.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man on long-term lithium therapy develops psoriasiform plaques. Among the following, which drug does NOT typically trigger or worsen psoriasis?
questions.exp: Cyclosporine is actually used to TREAT severe psoriasis (systemic immunosuppressant). Drugs that trigger or worsen psoriasis: lithium, beta-blockers (propranolol), antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, interferons, and abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids.

questions.q: A 20-year-old atopic child presents with severe eczema since infancy, recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, elevated IgE, and eosinophilia. The interleukin pathway primarily responsible for atopic dermatitis is:
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis is primarily a Th2-mediated disease driven by IL-4 and IL-13, which suppress skin barrier proteins (filaggrin, loricrin), promote IgE switching, and recruit eosinophils. Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα, blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling) is the first approved biologic for moderate-severe AD. This contrasts with psoriasis (Th17-mediated).

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman develops urticaria with angioedema every day for 8 weeks. She denies any allergic triggers. Physical examination is normal. Autologous serum skin test (ASST) is positive. What is the pathomechanism in this patient?
opts: IgG autoantibodies against FcεRI or IgE
Bradykinin excess from C1 esterase deficiency
questions.exp: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) lasting >6 weeks without identifiable trigger. A positive ASST indicates autoimmune urticaria — IgG autoantibodies against high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI) on mast cells (~40-60%) or against IgE itself. This causes mast cell activation independent of allergen. Treatment: second-generation antihistamines; omalizumab for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man on isotretinoin for severe nodular acne develops tenosynovitis, elevated liver enzymes, elevated triglycerides, and intracranial hypertension. Which side effect requires IMMEDIATE discontinuation of isotretinoin?
opts: Elevated AST to 2× upper limit of normal
questions.exp: Pseudotumour cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension) presenting with severe headache and papilloedema is a rare but serious complication requiring immediate discontinuation of isotretinoin. It is exacerbated by concurrent tetracycline use. Mild triglyceride elevation (<500 mg/dL) can be monitored; liver enzyme elevation <3× ULN may allow continuation with monitoring.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a recurrent BCC on the nose. What is the key advantage of this technique over standard wide local excision?
opts: It achieves 100% margin examination in horizontal frozen sections
It does not require local anaesthesia
It has lower recurrence rates because wider margins are taken
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery achieves the highest cure rates for BCC (>99%) and SCC because 100% of the peripheral and deep surgical margins are examined with horizontal (en face) frozen sections. This allows complete margin control while sparing maximum normal tissue, ideal for cosmetically sensitive areas. Standard excision examines only bread-loaf (vertical) sections, checking <1% of margins.
